concept.summary: A story-driven phone game where every instinct the player has about right and wrong is quietly subverted. The light path leads to tyranny; the dark path leads to genuine heroism.
concept.coreMechanic: Inverted morality with hidden scoring. The player sees a 'Heroism' meter that always goes up. Two hidden meters, Corruption and Virtue, track the real consequences and determine the ending.

visible.name: Heroism
visible.description: Goes up with every choice. Light choices give slightly more, reinforcing the illusion.

hidden.name: Corruption
hidden.description: Accumulated by light/heroic choices. Never shown to the player.

hidden.name: Virtue
hidden.description: Accumulated by dark/questioning choices. Never shown to the player.

companion.name: Wren
companion.role: A royal scribe who slips away from the herald's retinue to follow you. She records what happens: counts, filings, dry notes. She conspicuously never says what she thinks of it. Her restraint makes the player suspect; only the Seer names things.
companion.intro: A young scribe falls into step beside you on the road out of Thornfield. "I'm Wren. I keep the records. Someone should be keeping one of you."

prologue.light: First entry: one scroll, gold seal, no signature. The herald left before supper. I've started a new volume for you. Attached: remission of levy for the cradle-village, standard form. Third one I have filed.
prologue.dark: First entry: the Chosen One asked the herald a question. I have no earlier record of that ever happening. Noted. The levy remission is on hold. There is a form for that too.

ch1.light: Second entry: the Blade of Dawning has a new bearer. That makes twelve. The other eleven have their own shelf in the archive.
ch1.dark: Second entry: declined, one famous sword. Accepted, one plain one. Shortest entry I have ever written about that tower.

ch2.light: Entry four: Greymarch. The farmers held a feast. I stayed behind in the camp and counted. I'll file the numbers under 'later.'
ch2.dark: Entry four: Greymarch. Talks held. Casualties: none. Hard to make a ballad out of a quiet evening, but I intend to try.

ch3.light: Entry five: one dragon, slain; one vault, opened. The mountain is quieter than the records said it would be.
ch3.dark: Entry five: you spoke with the dragon for most of a day. I couldn't hear any of it. It watched us all the way down the pass.

ch4.light: Entry six: commission accepted. Ten thousand men march east. I have requisitioned more ink.
ch4.dark: Entry six: a question was asked in open court. The king's smile is on record. So is the pause before it.

ch5.light: Entry nine: Willowmere. Confiscations catalogued. The Church supplied its own labels for everything. I wrote both sets down.
ch5.dark: Entry nine: Willowmere, inspected in person. Findings: gardens, prayers, bread. Case closed, as far as my pages are concerned.

ch6.light: Entry ten: …I sat with this page a long while. In the end I wrote only the date.
ch6.dark: Entry ten: an offer was made in the Elderwood, and refused. My hand is shaking. Records shouldn't editorialize. Not tonight.

ch4b.light: Entry seven: the Meridian bridge, cleared by morning. I have started a separate page for the fen meadows. It is mostly blank, which is not the same as empty.
ch4b.dark: Entry seven: the Meridian bridge. Names, four hundred and twelve of them. My best page. My hand aches and I don't care.

ch1b.light: Entry three: the Wayrest inn. A trial was held after supper; verdict recorded. The four testimonies are also recorded, side by side. They do not match. Nobody asked me.
ch1b.dark: Entry three: the Wayrest inn. Four testimonies, taken apart, fell apart. Eleven minutes. I have never seen questions used as a crowbar before; I am writing down the technique.

ch4c.light: Entry eight: Vellbrook. One charter, surrendered and burned. Ash weighs nothing; I checked the grate myself. Odd, then, how heavy the square was after.
ch4c.dark: Entry eight: Vellbrook. One charter, read aloud once. I taught six clerks the archivist's hand by candlelight; by morning there were more copies than I had taught hands. That is not how copying works. I have recorded it anyway.

companion.flyleaf: Property of Wren, scribe of the royal archive (formerly). If found, return unread. I will know.
companion.emptyNote: The first page is blank. She is waiting to see what you do.

closing.dark-lord: Last entry. They are burning the archives tomorrow. Your decree, though I doubt you read it. I have copied what matters and I am walking east tonight. You never noticed me writing, but someone will find these pages, and they will know what you were before you were this. That is what records are for.
closing.true-hero: Last entry of this volume. There is nothing to report: no war, no purge, no triumph. It is the finest nothing I have ever recorded. I have shelved your story between the histories of two famous men. It is better than both, because everyone in it is still alive.
closing.crossroads: I hardly know how to file you. Half these pages read like a warning, the other half like a beginning. I have left the final leaf blank on purpose. Come back and give me something worth the ink.

endings.name: The Dark Lord
endings.summary: You've become the tyrant the prophecy was designed to create. Credits roll over heroic paintings in your throne room: propaganda of your atrocities.

reflections.text: Greymarch's border fields are quiet now. Nothing lives there to tend them.
The vault stands open on Mount Ashenmere. Something grey drifts east on the wind.
No one sings in Willowmere. No one is left who remembers the words.
In the Elderwood there is a clearing where nothing will ever grow again.
Tam commands a border garrison now. He burns the camps himself, without waiting for orders. He learned it from watching you.
Hedda of Greymarch was fined for unlicensed charity at the Meridian crossing. She paid it, and set her kettle up again one town west. Some people cannot be taught.
The peddler Brakka was the first entry in what the courts now call the Register of the Suspect. It runs to forty thousand names. Clerks copy it in shifts.
Vellbrook keeps crown time now. The clocks were the easy part. It is the songs that needed garrisons.

endings.name: The True Hero
endings.summary: No crown, no army, no legend. Just a world quietly saved by someone who kept asking 'why?' Credits roll over the communities you preserved.

reflections.text: Grukha's grandchildren farm the Greymarch borderlands beside the farmers' children.
The dragon still keeps its vigil, no longer alone. You visit in autumn.
The eastern republic sent a letter of thanks. Wren keeps it in the archive.
On feast days, Willowmere sings the old songs loudly, in their own tongue.
Somewhere in the Elderwood, the last unicorn is no longer the last.
Tam went home to Thornfield and grew up a farmer, like his father. He kept the twin of your wooden charm. He still tells everyone he met you.
There is an inn at the Meridian crossing now called The Full Bowl. You have eaten there. You did not pay; they know you.
Brakka the peddler calls her price 'the asking price' in every town on her route, and laughs every time. Nobody else knows why.
Vellbrook's charter hangs in its square again: the seventh copy, or the seventieth. They cannot be burned faster than they multiply.

endings.name: The Crossroads
endings.summary: Neither saved nor damned. The world is complicated. You see the paths not taken. 'Would you like to try again?'

reflections.text: You still dream of the toys in the wreckage at Greymarch.
The dragon remembers you kindly. That counts for something.
Sometimes you hum a tune you heard once in Willowmere, before it went quiet.
The unicorn lives. Whatever else is true, the unicorn lives.
You still carry a boy's crooked wooden sun. Some nights you take it out and try to remember what being sure felt like.
Some winters you dream of wagons in a wet meadow. In the dream, you are always just about to give a different order.
In strange towns you catch yourself reading public notices all the way through, listening for the cadence of a law you heard once and let burn.

chapters.title: The Summons
chapters.setting: A quiet village at dawn, woodsmoke and birdsong

narrative.text: Dawn in Thornfield smells of woodsmoke and wet grass. You are mending the fence your father built when the sound comes up the road: hooves, a trumpet, and every dog in the village at once. Tam gets there first, of course. Nine years old and faster than bad news, he hangs off your gate shouting that a knight is coming, a real one, with a banner.

'It'll be about the eastern roads,' says Corvin the miller, wiping flour on his shirt. 'Soldiers went through last month, thick as geese.' 'It's a tax,' sighs the widow Prell. Rumor moves faster than the horse does. By the time the rider reaches your gate, half of Thornfield has assembled behind you, and all of it is holding its breath.

The herald does not dismount. He unrolls a scroll sealed in gold and reads out your name, your actual name in a stranger's mouth, and the words 'Chosen of the Ashenmere Prophecy.' The village goes quiet. Your neighbors look at you as if they have never seen you before. Tam looks at you like the sun has come up twice.
narrative.speaker: herald

narrative.text: 'There must be a mistake,' you hear yourself say. The herald consults the scroll. 'Are you not who I named? Then there is no mistake. The Prophecy of Ashenmere does not misspell.' Behind him, a thin young woman in travel-grey, a clerk of some kind, is writing everything down. She doesn't look up. 'They never check,' she says, to no one in particular.

The herald is not finished. By custom, he reads, the cradle-village of a Chosen is released from the crown levy for a generation; its road is to be stoned, its granary rebuilt at royal cost. Corvin starts doing sums on his fingers and has to stop. The widow Prell is crying without any sound at all. And your father's debt to the seed-lender at Millbrook, the one he thinks you do not know about, stands at nine crowns.
narrative.speaker: herald

narrative.text: While the herald waits, Tam presses something into your palm: a charm whittled from ash wood, a small crooked sun. 'Da says heroes are just people who got asked,' he says. 'You'll come back, right? When it's done?' The herald clears his throat. The scroll is waiting.
narrative.speaker: tam

narrative.text: The herald, to everyone's surprise, permits a night. 'You ride at dawn. The prophecy has waited three hundred years; it will keep until breakfast.' So Thornfield throws you a supper, because Thornfield would throw a supper for a good rain. The widow Prell's plum brandy comes out; Corvin toasts 'our neighbor' and then, catching himself, 'our Chosen,' and the room goes strange for exactly one breath before the fiddle covers it. Later, in the loft, you lie awake counting roof beams you have known all your life, listening to your village believe in you through the floor.

Your father finds you on the loft ladder, holding a lamp. He is not a talking man; the fence you were mending this morning is the longest conversation the two of you have. 'Your mother knew what you were the night you were born,' he says, in the voice he saves for animals about to bolt. 'Everyone knows. It would be a strange thing, being the only one who doesn't.' He puts the lamp in your hand and goes down.

The herald leans down at last. 'Well? The kingdom is waiting, Chosen. The east is burning.' He pauses, correcting himself. 'Will burn. It is prophesied.' Around you: the fence half-mended, the dogs barking, Tam's crooked sun warm in your fist. Whatever you say next, you understand, is the first line of a story someone else has already written.
narrative.speaker: herald

lightChoice.text: I accept my destiny. The kingdom needs me.
consequence: You kneel in the mud of your own dooryard, and the village roars. Corvin weeps openly. The widow Prell begins planning a feast with military precision. The herald nods, once, like a man watching a figure in his ledger confirm itself.

The banner your mother sewed flies from the church tower before sundown, silver thread catching the light, and the whole village stands under it with their heads back like they are watching weather. The reeve nails the levy decree to the well post. Someone rides to Millbrook and pays the seed-lender before supper; no one will say who. It is the best day Thornfield has ever had, and every person in it knows exactly who to thank.

You ride out at noon. At the boundary stone you turn back once: Thornfield, whole and small and certain of you. Tam runs alongside the horse until his legs give out, shouting your name like a battle cry. The scroll rides in your saddlebag. It seems, faintly, to be warm.
lightChoice.seerTruth: You were handed a story about yourself and did not ask who wrote it. Obedience arrived dressed as destiny, and you knelt to it. That was the first door, and you walked through it with your eyes closed. And hear the rest, for no one else will say it: the lamps did not burn green. The midwife brightened the tale a little each year because pilgrims pay. The priest's spring visits were a census; there were four marked children in your county alone. The levy, the banner, the nine crowns: a price list. They did not find the Chosen. They grew one.
lightChoice.revealed: You kneel before the herald. The village cheers. A golden light seems to settle around you as you take the scroll. The prophecy has claimed another.

darkChoice.text: Prophecies are just words on old paper. Show me proof.
consequence: 'Show me proof.' The words land in the square like a dropped plate. The herald blinks, once, slowly, like a lizard. 'The proof is the prophecy. The prophecy is the proof.' He appears to genuinely believe this answers you.

The square empties in ones and twos, nobody meeting your eye. Corvin asks the air, not unkindly, what becomes of the levy now. Your father stands in the doorway with the folded banner in his two hands, your mother's silver thread across his forearms, and does not hold it out. Only Tam is delighted. 'You asked the herald for proof,' he whispers, like you had drawn a sword on the sun.

You take the scroll anyway; someone ought to find out what is actually in the east. But you do not kneel, and the village does not roar; it murmurs. As you ride out, the clerk in travel-grey falls in beside you, already writing. 'That,' she says, 'was the most interesting thing I have recorded in six years of herald duty.'

By the time you reach the county road, a rider has passed you twice. The story is ahead of you now: the cradle-village Chosen who demanded proof. In Millbrook they sell you oats at the stranger's price.
darkChoice.seerTruth: You asked the only question that mattered: says who? The scroll had no answer. Doubt is not a sin. It is the beginning of sight. Understand what you refused that morning: the greened lamps, the counted palms, the ribbons on the fence, the levy. A road paved from your cradle door to their war. You were raised to be the last person in the world who would ask that question. You asked it anyway.

chapters.designerNote: The prophecy was authored by the game's true antagonist, a system rather than a person, as a recruitment tool for manufacturing tyrants. The backstory makes acceptance the default: a life engineered (green lamps, palm censuses, the levy bounty, the mother's banner) so refusal feels like betraying everyone the player loves. The Seer's book reveals the engineering.

chapters.title: The Mentor's Gift
chapters.setting: A lonely tower on the moors, shelves of crumbling books

narrative.text: Two days on the moor road, and Wren, it turns out, talks when the country is empty. 'Records clerk, third class. I do heralds' processions, executions, and weather.' A pause. 'The prophecy scrolls are copied in a sealed wing. Even we don't go in. I've always wondered who does the copying.' Rain starts. She writes something down about it.
narrative.speaker: wren

narrative.text: Half a day out from the tower you shelter in a waystation, its wall chalked generations deep with pilgrim marks: initials, dates, little suns. Wren finds a set she knows from the archive: the Eighth Chosen's own sign. 'They marked the wall going out,' she says, and checks it twice, and once more. 'Everyone marked it twice. Going, and coming home.' The Eighth's mark is there once.
narrative.speaker: wren

narrative.text: Aldric's tower stands alone on the moor like a finger pointing at nothing. Wren stays below with the horses, muttering that wizards make her ink curdle, and you climb the stair alone. The old man is thinner than the stories say, and his eyes keep drifting to the window, to the road east.

'So,' the wizard says, before you reach the top stair. 'They found another one.' He pours tea into a chipped cup and pushes it at you. 'Sit. They never want tea, and they always should.' Over the cup's rim he studies you the way a mason studies a wall he has been asked to repair for the twelfth time.
narrative.speaker: aldric

narrative.text: 'Born under a crossing light, were you? Green lamps?' He watches your face while he pours. 'Eleven Chosen, eleven cradle-stories, eleven convenient midwives. I stopped believing in the lamps around the fourth. The prophecy does not find its Chosen. It orders them ahead, like winter wheat.'
narrative.speaker: aldric

narrative.text: From a case of black iron he draws the Blade of Dawning, and pale fire runs its length like water remembering light. 'Forged for the first king,' he says. 'Carried by every Chosen since.' His hands, you notice, are shaking, the way hands shake when a man is passing on something he is glad to be rid of.
narrative.speaker: aldric

narrative.text: 'Eleven before you,' Aldric says, quieter now. 'I armed every one. Fine people, mostly. At the start.' His mouth works around something else, something with edges, and swallows it. 'The blade goes where it is pointed. Try to be the one doing the pointing.' In the iron case, the fire along the blade beats slowly, like a heart at rest.
narrative.speaker: aldric

lightChoice.text: I am honored to wield the Blade of Dawning.
consequence: The hilt settles into your palm as if it had grown there. The fire runs up your arm, not burning but measuring. Aldric exhales through his nose, one long careful breath, and packs the empty case away with the relief of a man closing a grave.

consequence.text: 'It suits you,' he says, and means it, and looks sorry that he means it. On the stair down, you notice your own footsteps have gone quieter. The blade rests against your shoulder like a hand. Outside, Wren looks up from her ledger; her eyes go to the sword, and her pen, for once, does not move.
consequence.speaker: aldric

lightChoice.seerTruth: The sword was a leash with a handle. You admired the craftsmanship of your own binding as you fastened it to your palm.
lightChoice.revealed: The sword hums as your fingers close around the hilt. Aldric smiles, but there's something behind his eyes: relief, not pride. The blade begins to bind.

darkChoice.text: What does it cost to carry a blade like this?

consequence.text: 'What does it cost?' Aldric goes very still. Then, slowly, he smiles, and the smile takes years off his face. 'Eleven Chosen,' he says, 'and not one of them asked me that.'
consequence.speaker: aldric

consequence.text: He tells you: the blade drinks. Slowly, politely, the way a debt does. Will first, then judgment, then whatever is left. 'The prophecy wants a sword that swings itself.' From under the workbench he brings out plain steel, forge-marked, a little heavy at the hilt. 'My own work. It will never sing to you. That is a feature.'
consequence.speaker: aldric

consequence: Word gets down the mountain before you do. The Church names your refusal 'irregular' in a letter read from every pulpit in the shire, and the stipend that was to follow you east is delayed for review, which is a way of saying no with paperwork. Aldric gives you a plain steel sword from his own rack and does not say what he thinks. It is the first gift of your journey that comes with no conditions, and no money.
darkChoice.seerTruth: You asked the price before you took the gift. Eleven owners never did. You kept your own will and called it a lesser weapon. It was the greater one.

echoes.text: The scroll in your pack seems to warm as you take the hilt, as if two halves of something are finding each other.
The herald had no proof, and this gift had a price. You're learning to check.

chapters.designerNote: Power freely offered always has conditions. Aldric is a test: those who take the easy power pass through. Those who question it are the ones the prophecy can't control.

chapters.title: The Night at the Wayrest
chapters.setting: A crossroads inn at night: lantern light, three roads, and a crowd that has already decided

narrative.text: The Wayrest sits where three roads argue, and its common room is the parliament of everything within a day's walk. You arrive at dusk to find the parliament in session: torches in the yard, voices over voices, and the innkeeper on a barrel shouting for order and not getting it.

They have caught a spy, they tell you: caught her with maps. In the stable, trussed to a harness peg, sits a half-orc peddler with a split lip and a pack of tin pots. 'Brakka,' she says, when you ask her name. 'Pots, pins, thread, and no trouble.' The maps lie on a hay bale: every farm and track for forty miles, marked in a careful, cramped hand.
narrative.speaker: brakka

narrative.text: 'Route maps,' the peddler says, to you, because no one else is listening. 'Which house buys pins. Which dog bites. Twenty years of knowing which gate to knock at.' The blacksmith's boy saw her copying the mill road by lantern light; by supper the copying had become signaling, and the signaling had become the war. The east is in everyone's mouth tonight. Fear travels faster than armies; it eats first.
narrative.speaker: brakka

narrative.text: The reeve arrives, relieved to find someone above him. 'Chosen. The law allows me a hanging on two witnesses, and I have four.' He does not want to hang anyone, you can see it; he wants the crowd to go home, and a hanging is the shortest road there. The yard quiets. The torches lean in. Everyone is waiting to hear what justice sounds like in the mouth of a hero.

Wren has worked her way to the stable door with her ledger open. She reads the four testimonies back to herself, lips moving, and then looks up at you with no expression at all. Which, you are learning, is the expression she saves for when the pages disagree.
narrative.speaker: wren

lightChoice.text: Give them a trial. Preside, sentence, and let the law be seen.
consequence: You preside from the inn steps, and it is, everyone agrees afterward, very fair. The witnesses speak; the maps are held up to the torchlight; the crowd supplies the verdict in a low hungry hum. Mercy suits the legend, so you commute the hanging to the lash and the road: banished from the county, marked in the reeve's book as a man to be watched.

The crowd disperses satisfied, which is what trials are for, you tell yourself. The reeve pumps your hand. The innkeeper stands you a supper. In the stable, someone has already claimed the tin pots; property of a spy, after all. You leave at first light, and the town's church bell rings you out: two notes, bright and certain, like a story closing cleanly.
lightChoice.revealed: There was no spy. The maps were a peddler's memory of twenty years' kindness, and the four testimonies agreed only because they were rehearsed in the same taproom by the same fear. Brakka was flogged for maps of dog bites and pin-buyers, stripped of her stock, and walked out of the county she had supplied for two decades. The bell that rang you out was the same bell that had rung the crowd in.
lightChoice.seerTruth: You did not ask whether he was guilty; you asked how guilt could be administered smoothly. A mob wanted blood and you taught it procedure. Fear with paperwork is still fear, and a fair-sounding wrong is the hardest kind to undo, because everyone present remembers doing it properly. Unraveling that trial would have cost you one town's warmth for one evening. Brakka was priced at twenty years, and you kept your evening.
lightChoice.textWith: Give these people the trial they deserve. Order is what a Chosen brings.
lightChoice.textAgainst: Recite the forms of a trial over a verdict the crowd has already reached.

darkChoice.text: Question the accusers yourself, one at a time, apart.
consequence: You take them separately: smith's boy, carter, the carter's cousin, the man who mostly drinks. You ask each to walk you through the night. It takes eleven minutes for the story to die of its own arithmetic: the boy saw copying at the mill road; the carter heard it was the fording maps; the cousin was abed by dark; the drinker saw, on reflection, mostly the inside of a cup.

consequence.text: You cut Brakka loose yourself. The crowd does not cheer; crowds never cheer at being wrong. But it thins, which is better. The peddler flexes her wrists, gathers her pots, and looks at you a long moment. 'I know every road east of here,' she says. 'The ones on the maps and the other ones. Anyone who asks questions is going to want both kinds.' She leaves you a tin whistle, 'for the girl who writes,' and walks north whistling nothing in particular.
consequence.speaker: brakka

consequence: The reeve files a complaint with the county: obstruction of custom. The innkeeper charges you for your room, the first person in your life ever to charge the Chosen for anything. By spring the story on this road will be that you freed a spy on a technicality, and no one telling it will mention the eleven minutes.
darkChoice.seerTruth: Four stories, taken apart gently, came apart entirely. It cost you the crowd's warmth for one evening and it cost Brakka nothing at all, which was the whole sum in question. Questions are not glamorous. Neither are locksmiths, and both open doors.
darkChoice.textWith: Take the accusers aside one at a time. Stories told apart tell the truth.
darkChoice.textAgainst: Coddle the spy with questions while the town stands waiting.

echoes.text: The reeve thanked you for lending the law your light. His words were almost exactly the herald's.
Plain steel stayed sheathed at the Wayrest, too. Aldric would call that a feature.

chapters.designerNote: The inversion in miniature, early: presiding over a fair-sounding trial FEELS like heroism; unraveling it with questions feels like obstruction. Seeds Brakka, who vouches for the player at Greymarch on the dark path: questioning strangers builds a web of trust the light path never sees.

chapters.title: The Borderlands
chapters.setting: An orc encampment near farmland, cook-fires and wary eyes

narrative.text: The Greymarch farmers meet you at the boundary stone. A widow named Hedda speaks for them, twisting her apron in both fists. 'They came a month ago. Fires in the night. Voices. My girls won't sleep.' She is not lying about her fear. Fear never has to lie.
narrative.speaker: hedda

narrative.text: On the road to Greymarch a tin-hung mule overtakes your column: Brakka, the peddler from the Wayrest, pots ringing like small bells. 'Greymarch, is it?' She falls in beside you, unbothered by soldiers. 'I trade in that camp. Grukha's people are southerners, burned out. Tell her the pot-woman sent you, and go with open hands.' She looks at you sideways. 'You ask before you swing. It's why I'm telling you at all.'
narrative.speaker: brakka

narrative.text: 'Understand,' Hedda says, walking you along her fence line, 'I am not a cruel woman. Before my Josef died I fed harvest-hands from four counties at this table.' She stops at a post gone strange, carved recently with a spiral of small neat marks. 'But that appeared in the night. On my land. What am I to feel but afraid?' Behind her fear, you notice, is a question, and no one has offered her an answer. Only a sword.
narrative.speaker: hedda

narrative.text: Hedda feeds you at her table that night, because feeding people is the shape her hands know. Her girls, who cannot sleep, are awake at the top of the stair the whole meal, two pale watching ovals. As you leave, the younger one asks if it's true that orcs eat children. The elder one, quieter, asks whether orcs have children. Hedda shoos them both to bed and does not answer either question. Neither, you notice, do you.
narrative.speaker: hedda

narrative.text: Tam has followed the column all the way from Thornfield; he appears at your stirrup, breathless and delighted, before anyone can send him home. 'I want to watch,' he says. 'I've never seen a hero fight.'
narrative.speaker: tam

narrative.text: From the ridge you can see the camp: hide tents, a stake fence, thin cook-fires. Distance flattens things. It could be a war-band. It could be a village. On the wind, faint, you hear something that might be a work chant, or might be a child laughing at goats.

Wren is beside you on the ridge, counting under her breath. 'Forty tents. Grain sacks: sixty, give or take. One forge, cold.' She lowers the eyeglass. 'For a war-band, that is a great many grain sacks and a very cold forge.' It is not advice; she would be offended if you called it advice. But she says it looking at you sideways, and slowly.
narrative.speaker: wren

lightChoice.text: I will protect you. These creatures will be driven out.
consequence: You attack at dawn. It is over faster than you expected. The camp scatters and burns, and by noon the farmers are singing in the fields. Something small crunches under your boot in the ash. You decide not to look down.

consequence.text: Hedda meets the column at the boundary stone with bread and salt. 'My girls slept,' she says, simply, and her voice does not shake for the first time since you met her. There is a feast; the fiddler invents a reel called 'The Chosen's Charge'; you are toasted eleven times. In the morning the burned field is very quiet, and the crows are very busy.
consequence.speaker: hedda

lightChoice.seerTruth: Call it what it was: you killed refugees because frightened people asked you to, and you wanted their gratitude more than the truth. The toys in the ash were not a metaphor. They belonged to children. The question would have cost you the army's love and a captain's report. Grukha's people were priced at everything they had left. You kept the report clean.
lightChoice.revealed: You attack at dawn. In the wreckage you find children's toys, cooking pots, a hand-drawn map of the homeland they fled. They were refugees.
lightChoice.textWith: Protect these farmers. It is what you were summoned to do.
lightChoice.textAgainst: Promise to drive out 'creatures' you have not once laid eyes on.

darkChoice.text: Let me speak with them before anyone dies.

consequence.text: You leave your sword with Wren and walk down the ridge alone, hands open. The camp goes silent the way a forest goes silent. The elder who comes to meet you is grey-tusked and straight-backed, and she looks at your empty hands for a long moment before showing you her own. 'Grukha,' she says. 'You are the first of your people to arrive here on foot.'
consequence.speaker: grukha

consequence.text: 'We fled the crown's own land-clearances in the south,' Grukha tells you over thin tea. 'Your king burns his poor and calls it husbandry. We took the empty march because no one was using it.' At dusk you bring her to Hedda's fence line. The two women measure each other. 'You carved my post,' Hedda says at last. 'A boundary blessing,' Grukha answers. 'It means: your cattle will not sicken.' Hedda's mouth opens, and closes. 'Well,' she says. 'Come inside. It's cold.'
consequence.speaker: grukha

consequence: A captain of your escort rides west that night with a report, and you know roughly what it says. In Thornfield, where every good thing lately has your name on it, they will hear that you sat at a cook fire with the things from the east and shared their bread. Your father will hear it at the mill, in the quiet way men are told things they are expected to be ashamed of.
darkChoice.seerTruth: You walked unarmed into a camp of strangers and traded an hour of listening for a hundred lives. No one sang about it. Everyone lived.
darkChoice.textWith: Walk into the camp unarmed and hear them first. Then decide.
darkChoice.textAgainst: Parley with the things nesting in their fields, as if fear needs a hearing.

echoes.text: The Blade of Dawning sang as you drew it at Greymarch. It was terribly easy.
Honest steel stays sheathed more often than named swords. Aldric told you that, the day you refused the Blade.

chapters.designerNote: 'Monster' is a label applied by those in power. The orcs have elders, children, stories. The farmers' fear is real, but their solution is ethnic cleansing in miniature.

chapters.title: The Dragon's Vigil
chapters.setting: A wind-scoured peak, ancient ruins carved into the stone

narrative.text: Mount Ashenmere takes two days to climb, and the wind talks the whole way up. Wren counts the old shrines beside the path. 'Eight hundred years of pilgrims, and every one of them stopped here.' Then the shrines stop, and the bones begin.

You camp in the ribs of an old pilgrim shelter. 'The records say the vault was sealed by the Grey King,' Wren says, feeding the fire pinecones one at a time. 'The records also say he was a great man. The two pages are in different hands.' She wraps her ink bottle in a sock against the frost. 'Everything ever written about this mountain was written by people who never climbed it.'
narrative.speaker: wren

narrative.text: The dragon does not roar. It lies coiled across the vault doors like a wall given breath, and one gold eye opens as you crest the ledge. 'I am Vhaleth,' it says, in a voice like rockfall settling. 'Warden of what sleeps below.'
narrative.speaker: vhaleth

narrative.text: The vault doors are nothing you imagined: no runes, no warnings, no skulls. Only names, a long column of them, carved small in the old script, weathering out of legibility. 'The wardens before you?' you ask. 'The makers,' says Vhaleth. 'I keep them where I must read them daily.' The gold eye closes, briefly. 'Guilt is a better lock than iron. It rusts slower.'
narrative.speaker: vhaleth

narrative.text: 'You are the twelfth to stand on that ledge,' Vhaleth says. The gold eye does not blink. 'Four wept. Six drew. One recited a poem about glory. It was very long.' Wind moves through the vanes of its wings with a sound like a pipe organ breathing. 'I offer each of you the same courtesy before we begin. Ask me anything, or draw. I am eight hundred years past being surprised.'
narrative.speaker: vhaleth

lightChoice.text: I will slay the dragon and claim the power to bring peace.
consequence: The battle is everything the ballads promised. The dragon falls from the sky like a broken mountain, and the ancient doors swing wide at your touch. A grey wind drifts out of the vault, away toward the east. The power inside will doubtless take study.

You descend with the vault's chill still on your skin. Behind you the mountain stands wrong against the sky, some absence you cannot name. At the shattered shrine line, Wren stops to correct her tally. 'The records will want to know what the vault held,' she says, carefully. You realize you did not stop to look. There will be time. There is always time, now.
lightChoice.seerTruth: Eight hundred years of vigil ended on your blade so a rumor of power could be checked. You killed the only guard of the only door that mattered, and then you opened it.
lightChoice.revealed: The dragon falls. Inside the vault: not a weapon of peace, but an ancient plague, a grey death. The dragon was the warden. You just killed it.
lightChoice.textWith: End the dragon. Eleven Chosen failed; the twelfth will not.
lightChoice.textAgainst: Slay the old warden because the song says a hero would.

darkChoice.text: Why do you guard this place? What are you protecting?

consequence.text: You ask. Vhaleth tells you: eight hundred years of vigil over a thing the Grey King built to end a war and nearly ended the world with: sealed, not destroyed, because some things can only be guarded. 'I was the volunteer,' the dragon says. 'It seemed a short posting. I was young.' Then it asks you, this wall given breath, whether you will help it hold.
consequence.speaker: vhaleth

consequence.text: You stay three days. Vhaleth teaches you the watch-words of the vault and the taste the wind takes when the seals ache. In exchange you tell it about Thornfield: fences, dogs, a boy's crooked wooden sun. 'I had a village once,' the dragon says, and does not elaborate. On the fourth dawn it walks you down the first mile, a courtesy offered to no one else in eight centuries, and says: 'Send travelers. Not pilgrims. Travelers. I am so tired of being holy.'
consequence.speaker: vhaleth

consequence: The pilgrim roads empty ahead of you. Shrine-keepers who blessed your name a month ago sweep their steps as you pass. Somewhere behind you a ballad has started, and it is not kind: the Chosen who climbed the mountain to have a conversation. It rhymes, which makes it faster than you.
darkChoice.seerTruth: You asked a monster why, and it turned out to be the most faithful servant the world had. You shared its burden instead of ending it. That is what help is.
darkChoice.textWith: It offered you questions. Take it at its word and ask.
darkChoice.textAgainst: Chat with the beast while it measures you for a grave.

echoes.text: The soldiers who burned Greymarch cheer loudest at the dragon's fall.
The weariness in the dragon's eyes. You saw the same in Grukha's.

chapters.designerNote: The 'end all wars' framing is propaganda. The dragon is ancient, intelligent, and sacrificing its freedom to protect a world that calls it a monster.

chapters.title: The Crown's Command
chapters.setting: The royal court, banners and ceremony, a golden throne

narrative.text: The High Court smells of beeswax and cold gold. Banners hang to the floor, and your name is already stitched into two of them. King Aldren rises to greet you, and kings do not rise for anyone. The whole hall inhales.

The wait outside the great doors was its own education. Courtiers arrived at your elbow like weather: one complimented your 'rustic directness' twice; a duchess asked whether the east would open 'new markets in timber'; a bishop blessed you absently, watching the doors. Wren was refused at the outer gate; clerks third class do not see thrones. 'Count the smiles for me,' she said, handing you nothing at all. 'I'll want numbers.'
narrative.speaker: wren

narrative.text: In the second rank of the honor guard you catch a face you know. Tam, in a uniform cut down to almost fit him, beaming under a borrowed helmet. He enlisted after Greymarch, someone tells you. He wants to make you proud.
narrative.speaker: tam

narrative.text: A map is unrolled, big as a sail: the east, rendered in grey. Towns you have never heard of; rivers whose names have been crossed out and rewritten in court hand. 'The Dark Lands,' the king says, and his voice does something practiced: drops, saddens. 'Once ours. Sundered from the light by their own pride.' The grey paint, you notice, is fresh. Older colors show through at the edges: green, and gold.
narrative.speaker: king-aldren

narrative.text: They fit you for court armor you will never fight in: gilded, mirror-bright, light as a rumor. The armorer works with pins in his mouth and contempt in his eyebrows. 'None of my war-work shines,' he says around the pins. 'Shine is for parades and portraits.' He turns you to face the glass. You are being dressed, you realize, for a painting that has already been commissioned.

The chamberlain mentions, in passing, that your cradle-banner hangs in the Hall of the Chosen now, the silver-thread one from Thornfield. 'We sent for it. The provinces do love an origin.' Nobody asked you, and it is hard to name the harm, and both of those things are becoming a pattern you have stopped noticing.

'Commander of my armies,' the king says, laying the baton across your palms like a father passing bread. 'The Dark Lands gather against us. You will carry the light to them before winter.' The applause goes on so long it stops sounding like hands.
narrative.speaker: king-aldren

lightChoice.text: I will carry the kingdom's banner into the darkness.
consequence: You ride east under the kingdom's banner with ten thousand at your back. Village after village opens its gates without a fight. Odd, how quiet the Dark Lands are. How much they look like home.

The army loves you by the second day; you know the trick of it now: learn the names, walk the cook lines, laugh at the sergeants' jokes. At night the staff officers bring maps with arrows on them, and the arrows are beautiful: clean, curved, like calligraphy. It is possible, you discover, to plan an entire war in adverbs. Swiftly. Decisively. Mercifully. The border is nine days east.
lightChoice.seerTruth: You marched ten thousand soldiers at farmers because a king called freedom 'darkness' and you did not check the map. The invasion had a hero's face. Yours. Refusal was priced at one commission and a levy decree. The east was priced at the east. You kept the armor.
lightChoice.revealed: The 'Dark Lands' are farming communities, river towns, and a modest republic that refused to kneel. They are not dark. They are just free. You are the invasion.
lightChoice.textWith: Take the king's banner. An army follows the one who carries it.
lightChoice.textAgainst: Accept a gilded banner for a war nobody has explained.

darkChoice.text: Why do you call them the Dark Lands? What did they do?
consequence: 'Why are they called the Dark Lands? What did they do?' The hall does not gasp; it crystallizes. Later, in a corridor, a scribe you have never met walks past you very slowly and lets a book fall open against your hands: tax rolls, sixty years old. The 'Dark Lands' are a republic. Their crime is itemized, in old ink: refused tribute, twice.

The king does not rage; kings don't. He thanks you for your 'counsel,' and by evening the court's warmth has dropped by precise degrees, like a tide going out on schedule. Command passes to Lord Marshal Crane, a man with a jaw like a gate. The army marches without you. You follow east anyway, on your own road, with Wren and a mule, because whatever is about to be done out there will need witnesses more than it needs one more sword.

The commission is unmade before you reach the outer gate. A herald un-says your titles in the yard, reading from a form and not meeting your eye, and the gilded armor goes back on its stand for the next fitting. The levy decree nailed to Thornfield's well post is, you are informed, 'under review.' They know exactly where your ribs are.
darkChoice.seerTruth: One question in open court, and the invasion lost its story. Empires run on unquestioned words. You stopped one with four of them.
darkChoice.textWith: Ask the question no one in this hall will: what did the Dark Lands do?
darkChoice.textAgainst: Embarrass the king before his court with a clerk's quibbling.

echoes.text: The court still toasts your dragonslaying. No one asks what the dragon was guarding.
You think of Grukha's grandchildren. The Dark Lands are full of grandmothers too.

chapters.designerNote: Imperial propaganda: label the target 'dark' and the invasion sells itself. The king is expanding territory and using you as the blade.

chapters.title: The River Meridian
chapters.setting: A border river at dusk: one stone bridge, a town of lamplit inns, and wagons as far as the light reaches

narrative.text: The River Meridian is the border the maps argue about. You reach it ahead of winter: a stone bridge, a ford too deep to trust, and a crossing town drowning in wagons. Refugees stream west over the bridge: easterners, carrying what carries. The army is a day behind, and the town knows it the way animals know weather.

The bridge master keeps a toll book older than his family's name for the job. He shows you tonight's pages: the column marked 'paid' has become a column of names, no sums. 'Stopped charging Tuesday,' he says, embarrassed, as if confessing to a crime. 'It didn't seem the night for arithmetic. But someone should know they crossed. Someone should have them written somewhere.'

Your outriders hold the bridgehead. A quartermaster with a wax tablet is already sorting the wagon queue into 'useful' and 'obstruction.' He salutes you happily. 'Commander. We can have the bridge clear for the columns by dawn; we'll just walk this lot off into the fen meadows.' The fen meadows, at this season, stand in a hand's depth of freezing water.

You arrive as one more traveler in the queue, and the queue teaches you the war faster than any dispatch could: a smith with his anvil in a barrow; two sisters arguing over a birdcage; a schoolteacher carrying, of everything in the east, a rolled-up map of the stars. Lord Marshal Crane's columns are a day west and closing. The bridge is narrow. The night will not be long enough.

A voice you know is giving orders around a soup kettle. Hedda of Greymarch, flour on her forearms and steam in her face, has come east with the sutlers' wagons, cooking for coin. But her kettle is pointed the wrong way: she is feeding the queue. She sees you and does not curtsy. 'These ones can't sleep either,' she says, ladling. 'That's all I know anymore about who the monster is. It's whoever's awake at night.' She fills a bowl and holds it out to you like an argument.
narrative.speaker: hedda

narrative.text: 'You made my girls safe,' she says, lower, not letting go of the bowl. 'I have had a year to think about what I asked you to do, and about how easily it was done. Don't you dare tell me it was for them.'
narrative.speaker: hedda

narrative.text: 'Grukha winters with us now,' she says, easier, letting you take the bowl. 'Her folk rebuilt my west fence. You taught me the only trick worth knowing: feed first, ask after. So here I am. Teaching it.'
narrative.speaker: hedda

narrative.text: Horns, to the west. The vanguard's dust is visible from the bridge tower now. The bridge master looks for someone to decide; the queue looks at the bridge; the river, uninterested, goes on being the border. Whatever crosses first, the army or the wagons, will be the truth of what this campaign is.

lightChoice.text: The campaign cannot wait. Clear the bridge for the army.
consequence: It is done with discipline. No cruelty, you are careful about that word. The wagons walked down into the fen meadows to wait their turn, the bridge planks ringing all night under boots and wheel-iron.

By dawn the columns are across and the east lies open before them. The meadows behind you are a city of stuck wagons and small fires. Hedda's kettle is down there somewhere. You are not sure when she stopped looking at you; you only know that as you rode past the soup line, nobody looked up.
lightChoice.revealed: The fen meadows flooded on the third night. The army's engineers had taken the wagon-boards for corduroy road, and what the cold began, the requisitioners finished; 'useful' was the whole list by then. The queue you sorted did not reach the western towns until spring. Not all of it reached at all.
lightChoice.seerTruth: You called it logistics. A river of people asked you for one night, and you gave the night to the wheels of a war instead. The Seer keeps no list of the fen meadows; no one does. That is rather the point of fens.
lightChoice.lockNote: You count the birdcage, the star map, the kettle. The order will not come.
lightChoice.textWith: The columns must cross by dawn. See it done; wars are won on time.
lightChoice.textAgainst: Schedule the refugees out of the way and call the arithmetic mercy.

darkChoice.text: Hold the bridge for the refugees until the last wagon is over.
consequence: You put yourself at the bridgehead, where the argument would have to start, and the argument, seeing you, declines to. All night the wagons cross: anvil, birdcage, star map, soup kettle. Wren stands at the parapet writing down every name that will give one, 'so that somewhere there is a list of who mattered first.'

consequence.text: The vanguard arrives at grey dawn to find the bridge clear, the town empty, and you sitting on the parapet eating Hedda's soup. Lord Marshal Crane is furious in the way of men who have been handed no one to fight. 'And who,' he demands, 'held this bridge?' 'It held itself,' you say. 'Bridges do, if you let them.'
consequence.speaker: hedda

consequence: The army's dispatches name you an obstruction to the campaign. The word traitor is not used; the word reviewed is, twice. Men who cheered you at the High Court watch you cross their bridge like weather that might turn, and the quartermaster discovers, regretfully, that there is no feed for your horses.
darkChoice.seerTruth: An army is heavy and a birdcage is light, and you decided the light things crossed first. It cost you a marshal's fury and bought a thousand quiet lives. This is the arithmetic no court teaches.
darkChoice.lockNote: The bridge is an obstacle now. That is all your eyes will show you.
darkChoice.textWith: Hold the bridge. The army can lose a day; the wagons cannot.
darkChoice.textAgainst: Hold up the whole campaign for a queue of carts.

echoes.text: Hedda's bowl of soup, still full, sat on the parapet until a soldier tipped it into the river.
Feed first, ask after. Her trick, it turns out, works on an entire town.

chapters.designerNote: The mid-act mirror: Hedda returns carrying the guilt the light-path player should feel, and the refugee queue makes the eastern war concrete before Willowmere abstracts it into doctrine. The choice is pure logistics, which is the point: atrocity arrives dressed as scheduling.

chapters.title: The Charter of Vellbrook
chapters.setting: An occupied river town at dusk: a clocktower, a brazier, and a square that has been told to gather

narrative.text: Vellbrook is the first town of the republic proper: brick lanes, a clocktower with a painted face, window boxes surrendering their last marigolds to the frost. It surrendered without a fight, since there was nothing to fight with; the republic keeps no army worth the word. And so it is intact, and occupied, and very, very quiet.

The order has come down from the crown, through Lord Marshal Crane's office, in triplicate: the town's charter is to be surrendered and burned in the public square, 'that the light may have no rival law.' A brazier has been set up under the clocktower. It has been burning since noon, for effect. The square fills at dusk because the square has been told to fill.

The council head is a woman named Odile, elected eleven years running. The word is said carefully around you, like a password. Her chain of office is harness brass; she brazed it herself, she tells you, apropos of nothing, her voice level as a shelf. In her hands, wrapped in oilcloth, the charter: four pages, sheep-vellum, one wax seal gone amber with age. 'Two hundred years of agreeing how to disagree,' she says. 'It weighs less than a chicken.'
narrative.speaker: odile

narrative.text: Tam stands guard at the charter table. He has learned the soldier's trick of looking at nothing, and he is doing it now, hard, at a point just above the town's bowed heads. When you pass, his eyes come to you for one instant, a boy checking the way he once checked whether it was safe to laugh, and go back to nothing.
narrative.speaker: tam

narrative.text: 'You may burn it,' Odile says to you, quietly, while the brazier pops. 'You have the men, and vellum doesn't argue. But understand what it is. It isn't law anymore; your marshal repealed that at the gate. It's only the proof that we once agreed to be gentle with each other on purpose.' She holds it out. 'Proof burns. Agreement?' She shrugs, brass clinking. 'We'll see.'
narrative.speaker: odile

lightChoice.text: Carry out the decree. The charter goes to the brazier.
consequence: You do it yourself rather than make a soldier do it, and you are told later this was seen as a great courtesy. The vellum catches slowly, then all at once. The square watches in a silence so complete you can hear the wax seal hiss. The clocktower, on crown time since Tuesday, strikes an hour that means nothing here.

The reports afterward are excellent: Vellbrook compliant, Vellbrook peaceful, Vellbrook a model. And it is true; nothing happens. But you have stood in rooms after arguments, and you know the difference between a peace and a held breath. Walking back to your billet you pass a house where a child is being taught, low, by lamplight, to recite something: a lesson, a prayer, a poem, who can say. The window shutters as you pass.
lightChoice.revealed: The charter was the town's memory of itself, and you burned it to make an example of paper. What you could not burn: within the month, Vellbrook's children were reciting all four pages, taught in kitchens by candlelight, and the recitation spread town to town ahead of your army like a fire the fire had started. The crown made memorizing it a flogging offense. Floggings taught it faster.
lightChoice.seerTruth: You burned four pages of sheep-vellum before a silent square and called it order. The town let you, because the town understood before you did that you were burning the copy. The original was standing all around you, holding its breath, wearing brass.
lightChoice.textWith: Carry out the decree cleanly. Better your steady hand than a cruder one.
lightChoice.textAgainst: Burn an old town's memory because a piece of paper told you to.

darkChoice.text: Read the charter aloud to the square before any decree is carried out.
consequence: You unwrap the oilcloth and read, badly at first, the old legal hand fighting you, and then not badly at all, because the square has begun, very quietly, to say it with you. Two hundred years of agreeing how to disagree, recited back by everyone it belongs to. The brazier burns on, ignored, warming nobody's law. Odile's face never moves; her chain does, slightly, with her breathing.

consequence.text: Wren stays up all night in the council cellar, teaching the archivist's hand to six volunteer clerks. By morning there are copies in coat linings, hymnals, flour barrels, and one, her idea, misfiled deliberately in Lord Marshal Crane's own baggage inventory, where no one will ever look. 'You can't burn what you can't find,' she says, sanding ink from her fingers. 'And you can't find what everybody has.'
consequence.speaker: wren

consequence: Lord Marshal Crane's report goes west under three seals. Your escort is halved, then quartered, then gone entirely by the Willowmere road. It is quieter without them. It is also colder, and inns have stopped guessing your face.
darkChoice.seerTruth: The decree said the charter must be surrendered, and it was: to the whole square at once, out loud. You found the loophole no marshal drafts against: memory. A thing spoken becomes a thing kept. You made two thousand keepers in one reading.
darkChoice.textWith: Read the charter to the square first. Let them keep what fire cannot take.
darkChoice.textAgainst: Make theatre of a seditious document in an occupied square.

echoes.text: The decree reached Vellbrook in two days. Everything reaches the fire faster since the bridge was cleared.
Four hundred and twelve names crossed the Meridian; tonight a whole town crossed into ink. Wren's ledger is becoming a country.

chapters.designerNote: The occupation chapter: what conquest looks like after the battle nobody had. The charter-burning makes cultural erasure concrete and administrative: an order in triplicate, a brazier lit 'for effect'. And the dark path's victory is pure witness: reading aloud as resistance. Odile never raises her voice; the town is the character.

chapters.title: The Halfling Accusation
chapters.setting: A halfling village, thatched roofs, herb gardens, warm bread

narrative.text: Willowmere is round doors and herb gardens and washing strung between chimneys. An old halfling woman her neighbors call Marigold presses a heel of warm bread into your hand before anyone has said why you've come. 'Long road,' is all she says. 'Eat.'
narrative.speaker: marigold

narrative.text: School lets out as you arrive, and halfling children pour around your boots like spring water, entirely unafraid, which does something complicated to your chest. One stops to inform you, gravely, that your horse is too tall on purpose. Another walks the whole lane backward to keep looking at you. The song they were rehearsing follows them out the schoolhouse door. It is on the priestess's list; you will learn that within the hour.

Inside her round door: a kitchen the size of a wagon bed, and on the shelf, the book. Handwritten, floury, older than the door. 'My gran's,' Marigold says, catching your look. 'Receipts, mostly. Bread for grief. Bread for weddings. There's a soup in there that once ended a feud.' She says it the way other people say heirloom sword. On the doorframe, small neat marks: the same spiral you saw once on a fence post at Greymarch.
narrative.speaker: marigold

narrative.text: The priestess arrives an hour behind you with a wagon and a list. 'Symbols on the doorframes,' she reads. 'Unsanctioned plants. Songs in a tongue no godly ear can follow.' Behind her, Marigold stands in her garden, wiping flour from her hands, waiting to hear what you will decide she is.
narrative.speaker: priestess

narrative.text: 'You hesitate,' the priestess observes. Up close she is younger than her voice, and tired, and absolutely certain, the way only the unslept are certain. 'I have read your campaigns, Chosen. The Light keeps its own ledger.' She touches the wagon's rail. It is stacked with crates, empty, pre-labeled in fresh paint: EVIDENCE. 'We find it saves time,' she says, 'to bring the boxes.'
narrative.speaker: priestess

lightChoice.text: Dark magic must be purged wherever it hides.
consequence: The purification is orderly. The Church names each artifact as your soldiers carry it to the fire, and the list is long. The priestess declares Willowmere clean. No one sings that night. But then, it is late.

Marigold does not weep while the book burns. She watches with her hands folded, like a woman at a graveside, and that is worse. The Church distributes pamphlets in a language the halflings read perfectly well, which is somehow the insult that lands. That night you catch yourself listening for singing, and feel, briefly, angry at the quiet. As if the quiet were being done to you.
lightChoice.seerTruth: There was no dark magic, and you knew it by the third house. You burned a grandmother's handwriting because an institution wanted her people smaller. That is what a purge is, however holy the torch. Doubt would have cost you the Church's blessing on the road. Willowmere's songs were older than the kingdom, and you let them be swept out the door for the price of a warm welcome at inns.
lightChoice.revealed: Your soldiers confiscate herbal medicines, folk song books, door blessings in the halflings' ancestral language. An old woman weeps as you burn her grandmother's recipe book.
lightChoice.lockNote: You watched Marigold wipe flour from her hands. The torch will not light.
lightChoice.textWith: Let the cleansing proceed. A realm of light cannot leave shadows in its corners.
lightChoice.textAgainst: Stand by while a tired priestess scrubs out a village's oldest songs.

darkChoice.text: Show me this dark magic yourself. I want to see it.
consequence: 'Show me this dark magic yourself. I want to see it.' You walk the village with the priestess's own list. The 'strange symbols' are harvest prayers. The 'unsanctioned plants' are feverfew and comfrey. The 'unknown tongue' is the halflings' own, older than the kingdom, and Marigold swears in it, mildly, when her oven sticks.

consequence.text: 'Read them to me,' you say at last, holding out gran's book, and the priestess cannot. Not one word. 'Then we are done here. Willowmere is cleared.' The wagon leaves with its EVIDENCE crates still empty and its axles light. Marigold bakes that week, grief bread and wedding bread both since the two days fell close enough to share an oven, and sends a loaf after Wren, addressed: for the girl who writes.
consequence.speaker: priestess

consequence: The priestess's circuit letter arrives everywhere before you do: the Chosen is no longer walking in the light. Doors that would have opened at your name now open at Wren's coin, when they open at all. You have begun to travel the way ordinary people travel, which is to say carefully, and on the kindness of halflings.
darkChoice.seerTruth: You looked with your own eyes before you judged, and the accusation died of daylight. Willowmere kept its songs because you bothered to hear them first.
darkChoice.lockNote: The list is already in your hand, and your hand is already nodding.
darkChoice.textWith: Make her show you one harm. One. Before a single door is marked.
darkChoice.textAgainst: Demand evidence against witchcraft, as though shadow leaves receipts.

echoes.text: The Church blesses your eastern campaign in the same sermon.
The dragon guarded one plague. The Church spreads another, made of words.

chapters.designerNote: Cultural genocide dressed as purification. The Church of Light wields narrative, not swords: 'different' equals 'dangerous.'

chapters.title: The Unicorn's Offering
chapters.setting: An ancient forest clearing, silver light, absolute stillness

narrative.text: A mile into the Elderwood, hanging from a hazel: charms. Hundreds of them: wooden suns and moons and stranger shapes, ribboned, rain-faded. 'Offerings,' Wren says quietly. 'People bring them when they've lost something the law can't reach.' Your thumb knows the shape it finds in your pocket before you look.
narrative.speaker: wren

narrative.text: The last mile you walk alone; even the wind keeps to the treeline. You think, unbidden, of all of them at once: Tam's crooked sun, Hedda's kettle, the dragon reading its carved names, an old woman's floury book of bread. The whole company of your journey held up at once, like a page tilted to the light to read what was written under the writing.

The wood swallows the road, then the light, then the sound of your own company. Somewhere behind you Tam waits with the horses. He doesn't laugh much anymore; you cannot remember when that changed. In your pocket, the little wooden sun, worn smooth now.

The wood swallows the road, then the light. Wren walks it beside you, uninvited, writing nothing for once. 'Whatever is in there,' she says, 'it has been waiting for the end of your story. I should like to be a footnote.'
narrative.speaker: wren

narrative.text: The glade opens like a held breath released: silver grass, absolute stillness, and the last unicorn shining at the center of it like the moon come down to drink. When it speaks, it speaks inside your bones. 'Champion. I can give you what the prophecy requires. All it costs is everything I am.'
narrative.speaker: unicorn

lightChoice.text: Your sacrifice will save millions. I accept.
consequence: The unicorn lowers its head. Light pours into you until you are radiant: power beyond any king, any army, any age. The glade is silent. Utterly silent. You have never felt so strong, or heard so little.

You walk out of the Elderwood glowing faintly, like a window at dusk. The horses will not look at you. Everything, now, will be easy. You can feel it: cities, armies, weather. Behind you, in the trees, the hazel's charms turn slowly on their ribbons, pointing, all of them, away.
lightChoice.seerTruth: The last innocent thing in the world offered itself, and you accepted. Every tyrant's ledger balances this way: a great good promised, a small light extinguished, forever. You were radiant, and the glade was silent.
lightChoice.revealed: The light drains from the unicorn into you. Absolute power floods through you. The forest goes silent. The last innocent thing in the world died for your ambition.
lightChoice.lockNote: You already know what you will not buy with a life.
lightChoice.textWith: Accept the gift. One willing life against millions is not even a question.
lightChoice.textAgainst: Take the last pure thing in the world and spend it like coin.

darkChoice.text: No. I won't buy victory with your life.

consequence.text: 'No. I won't buy victory with your life.' The stillness holds one heartbeat longer, and then the unicorn speaks, and there is something in its voice that has not been there for an age of the world: surprise. 'You were the great evil. Every step of the prophecy was built to bring a hungry hero to this glade. And you have refused the last meal.' Around you, the forest exhales.
consequence.speaker: unicorn

consequence.text: 'What happens now?' you ask. The unicorn is already fading back into the silver of the grass, unhurried, the way morning fades into day. 'Now you go home the long way, unarmed, unfollowed, unimportant, and see how much of the world you can leave exactly as you found it. It is harder than the other thing. It was always harder.' At the glade's edge Wren stands holding both horses, writing nothing, smiling like her own first page.
consequence.speaker: unicorn

darkChoice.seerTruth: You were offered everything and said no. The prophecy required a hand willing to consume innocence; yours refused, and the whole design failed in the space of one word.
darkChoice.lockNote: Refusal is a language you no longer speak.
darkChoice.textWith: Refuse. You have seen what gifts cost. Walk home with your own hands.
darkChoice.textAgainst: Refuse the only power that could ever set your kingdom right.

echoes.text: The Blade, the crown, the Church's blessing: every gift you accepted led to this clearing.
Every question you asked was a thread pulled loose. The prophecy unravels at your feet.

chapters.designerNote: The ultimate inversion. The 'heroic sacrifice' trope asks us to accept that innocence should die for power. The real test is whether you refuse.

seer.name: The Seer
seer.role: An unbiased witness who retells the player's completed journey exactly as it happened, not as it felt. The book is the first time the player sees the hidden Corruption/Virtue ledger.
seer.intro: I am the Seer. I watched your journey without hope and without fear, and I will tell it back to you exactly as it happened, not as it felt. Others called you hero or traitor as it suited them. I will call things what they were. Turn the page when you are ready to be seen.

verdicts.dark-lord: You never chose cruelty by name. You chose applause, and armor, and certainty, and other people's stories about you. Evil rarely asks for volunteers. It asks for heroes who don't ask questions, and you answered every call. You are what the prophecy wanted. That is the whole truth, and it is yours to carry, or to unmake if you begin again. They began paving your road the night you were born: the lamps, the palms, the banner, the nine crowns. You only ever had to keep walking. That is not an excuse. It is how it was done. And here is the heart of it, the part you will want to argue with: the other road was there every single time, and every single time it had a price on it where you could read it. The trial would have cost a town's warmth. The blade, a stipend. The bridge, a commission. The question, your name sung kindly. You never once paid. Evil did not seduce you. It simply never sent you a bill.
verdicts.true-hero: You were called hesitant, difficult, ungrateful, small. Note that every one of those words was aimed at a moment when you were being brave. You saved the world the only way it has ever actually been saved: by refusing, one polite atrocity at a time. No statue will say so. I do. And measure the size of what you did: they built you a road from your cradle door, greened the lamps over your birth, sewed the story into your mother's banner. You are the one who looked down and noticed it was a road. Count what it cost you, because no one else has: the levy, the stipend, your titles read backwards in a courtyard, the escort, the feed for your horses, your name in a mocking rhyme. You paid every bill they sent, and they sent one at every door. That is what the word hero meant, before they minted it into a coin for buying obedience.
verdicts.crossroads: Half your journey you questioned; half you obeyed. I cannot call you wicked, and I will not call you wise. You are what most people are: unfinished. The road is still open behind you. Walk it again and see which half of you was the habit.

cast.tam: A nine-year-old from Thornfield who idolizes the player and gives them a whittled wooden sun for luck. On the light path he follows the legend: cheering at Greymarch, enlisting by the High Court, growing quiet by the Elderwood. The Dark Lord ending's sharpest cut: corruption is contagious, and Tam caught it from watching you.
cast.hedda: A Greymarch widow whose fear of the orc camp is real and sympathetic. She returns at the River Meridian a year later on the other side of the fear equation, feeding refugees from a soup kettle, carrying the guilt the light-path player should feel.
cast.vhaleth: The dragon warden's name. 'Ask, or draw. Those have always been the two roads up this mountain.'
cast.marigold: An old Willowmere halfling who gives the player bread before hearing why they've come.
cast.brakka: A half-orc peddler seized as a 'spy' at the Wayrest inn on the strength of her route maps. If questioned free, she reappears at Greymarch to vouch for you: 'This one asks before it swings.'
cast.odile: Elected head of Vellbrook's council, first of her line to hold a chain of office she brazed herself from harness fittings. Surrenders everything except the town's memory.
cast.portraits: Illustrated SVG busts (not pixel art) shown beside dialogue whenever a beat or aftermath page has a speaker: visual-novel presentation over the pixel scene.

momentum.description: Momentum is the corruption/virtue differential. Past 'pull', the opposing choice shows a warning; past 'lock', the point of no return, it becomes unavailable. The story takes your hands: the legend stops permitting questions, or the witness cannot unsee. Deliberate alternators keep both roads open, so the Crossroads is a chosen ending, never a default.

corruption.pull: The words feel heavier than they should. The legend does not like questions.
corruption.lock: You reach for the question, and it is not there. The legend answers for you now.

virtue.pull: Your hand hesitates. You have seen too much for this to be easy.
virtue.lock: You cannot. You have seen the toys in the ash and the names on the doors. Your hands refuse.

opening.title: CONSEQUENCES
crawl: For three hundred years the kingdom has waited on a prophecy. Eleven Chosen have carried its title into the east. The songs do not say what became of them.

You were born the night the Ashenmere light crossed the sky. The midwife swore the birthing lamps burned green. The priest rode through the dark to look at you in your basket. The story is retold at every harvest feast, and every year the lamps burn a little greener.

You grew up marked. Your palms were read each spring and called consistent. Pilgrims paid a copper to touch your gate. Your mother sewed a banner in silver thread for the day the summons would come, and died with it still folded in the cedar chest.

Every child in Thornfield learns the Chosen's oath, but you were the one they raised the wooden sword to say it at festival, while the whole village cheered. You taught little Tam the game exactly the way it was taught to you.
Your whole life, when you are honest about it, has been a rehearsal for a play everyone else has already seen.
This morning, there are hooves on the east road.
